article.overview: An X-ray detector is an instrument that records X-ray photons arriving from a source. On the Moon, X-ray detectors are used mainly to identify the chemical elements present in surface rock and soil, and to study X-rays produced by the Sun. The name describes a class of instruments rather than a single design. The examples in this article use X-ray fluorescence: solar X-rays strike the surface, the surface emits element-specific X-rays, and a detector in lunar orbit measures them.
article.description: In lunar science, an X-ray detector usually measures photons in a defined energy band. The instruments discussed here cover roughly 0.5 keV to 20 keV. Each detected photon produces a signal whose size relates to its energy, and the energy identifies the element that emitted it. Counting these photons over a surface region gives an elemental map. Two X-ray sources matter at the Moon: fluorescent X-rays emitted by the surface when it is illuminated by solar X-rays, which are strongest during solar flares, and X-rays from the Sun itself. Detector technologies have included gas-filled proportional counters, silicon solid-state detectors and swept charge devices. Each design trades energy resolution, collecting area, field of view and mass against one another.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of lunar X-ray spectroscopy is to measure the abundance of major rock-forming elements, especially magnesium, aluminium and silicon, and where possible calcium, titanium and iron. Ratios such as Mg/Si and Al/Si help scientists interpret rock composition across the surface, which supports studies of crustal formation and evolution. Because fluorescence depends on the incoming solar X-ray spectrum, instruments typically include a solar monitor so that the measured fluorescence can be calibrated and converted into absolute abundances [2][3][4]. Orbital maps also reveal spatial variations in composition that cannot be seen from a limited set of returned samples.
article.operating_principle: When an X-ray photon is absorbed in a detector, it produces a measurable electrical pulse whose size is proportional to the photon energy. In a gas-filled proportional counter, the photon ionises the gas inside a chamber with a thin entrance window. The Apollo 15 and 16 instruments used proportional counters with beryllium windows [1][2]. The Chandrayaan-1 C1XS used swept charge device sensors operating near room temperature, behind collimators and filters [4]. Collimators define the field of view and therefore the surface footprint, while filters block lower-energy X-rays so that a detector responds to a chosen band. Surface elements emit characteristic lines at known energies. The principal K-alpha lines of magnesium, aluminium and silicon lie at 1.254, 1.487 and 1.740 keV respectively [2], so the energy spectrum identifies the element and the line intensity relates to its abundance.
article.scientific_importance: Lunar elemental maps are important because the Moon's crust and mantle record its early differentiation, later volcanism and impact history, and surface composition can be measured remotely over areas that no sample has reached. X-ray fluorescence measures major elements such as magnesium, aluminium and silicon directly from orbit. The Apollo 15 and 16 instruments mapped Mg, Al and Si along their ground tracks [1][2]. Later orbital instruments, including ISRO's C1XS and the Chandrayaan-2 CLASS instrument, extended the approach with newer detector technology [4][5][6]. Fluorescence results depend on solar X-ray input, which varies with solar activity, so measurements are concentrated in periods of higher solar activity. Re-analysis of earlier data with improved calibration is also possible, as the 2021 re-evaluation of the Apollo observations shows [2].

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal mass, size or power figure for an X-ray detector. The figures below apply only to the named instruments or pre-launch designs. Where a value could not be verified from a source reviewed for this article, it is marked as not publicly specified.

examples.name: Apollo 15 and 16 X-ray Fluorescence Spectrometer (XRFS)
examples.type: Historical lunar orbital instrument, flown on the Command Service Module of Apollo 15 and Apollo 16
examples.summary: The XRFS was carried on the Command Service Module and mapped chemical elements along the ground tracks of the spacecraft using sunlight-induced X-ray fluorescence [1][2]. The NASA PDS archive documents the Apollo 16 instrument [1]. The 2021 re-evaluation summarises the hardware, orbit and data parameters used here [2].

specifications.Detectors: Three proportional counters plus a separate solar monitor, all proportional counters [2]
specifications.Windows: Beryllium window of approximately 25 micrometres per detector, effective window area about 25 square centimetres [2]
specifications.Filters: Detector 2 carried a magnesium filter and detector 3 an aluminium filter. The filter thicknesses assumed in the 2021 analysis are stated as uncertain in the literature [2]
specifications.Field of view: About +/-30 degrees (full width at half maximum), set by collimator cells [2]
specifications.Energy channels: Eight channels. In normal mode, channels 1 to 7 cover 0.69 to 3.0 keV and channel 8 covers above 3.0 keV. Extended mode covers 1.4 to 6.0 keV on detector 1 [2]
specifications.Elements: Mg, Al and Si from K-alpha lines at 1.254, 1.487 and 1.740 keV. Ca and Fe were covered in extended mode, but those maps were of low quality and are not discussed [2]
specifications.Orbit altitude: About 20 to 100 km during the first part of each mission, then about 100 to 120 km [2]
specifications.Map footprint: About 60 by 75 km for low-altitude orbits and 110 by 125 km for high-altitude orbits [2]
specifications.Solar monitor: Measured the Sun's X-ray output at the same time as the surface detectors, mounted on the opposite side of the CSM. Apollo 15 used one beryllium window; Apollo 16 used two after gain shifts were seen on Apollo 15 [2]
specifications.Mass, dimensions, power: Not verified in the sources reviewed; not publicly specified here [1][2]

examples.name: SMART-1 Demonstration of a Compact Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (D-CIXS) with X-ray Solar Monitor (XSM)
examples.type: Lunar orbital instrument on ESA's SMART-1 mission; specifications are from pre-launch design tables
examples.summary: D-CIXS was an X-ray spectrometer designed to map lunar elemental composition from orbit on ESA's SMART-1 mission [3]. The XSM monitors the solar X-ray input, the same calibration role that the solar monitor played on Apollo [2][3]. The ESA mission table gives mass and power for the two instruments together, not separately [3].

specifications.Detector (D-CIXS): Swept charge device detectors, energy range 0.5 to 10 keV [3]
specifications.Field of view (D-CIXS): 12 by 32 degrees in the design table; the axis order differs from a figure in the same source [3]
specifications.Spatial resolution: 50 km for the planned map product [3]
specifications.Spectral resolution: Not stated in the source table [3]
specifications.Detector (XSM): Silicon PIN detectors, energy range 0.8 to 20 keV, field of view 104 degrees [3]
specifications.Mass and power: 5.2 kg and 18 W for D-CIXS with XSM together; separate values not stated [3]
specifications.Status of values: Pre-launch design values that may not match the flight unit [3]

examples.name: Chandrayaan-1 X-ray Spectrometer (C1XS) with X-ray Solar Monitor (XSM)
examples.type: Lunar orbital instrument on India's Chandrayaan-1 mission
examples.summary: C1XS was based primarily on the D-CIXS design. ESA funded it primarily, with partial ISRO support, and the hardware was developed at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory with the ISRO Satellite Centre [4]. It measured X-ray fluorescence from the lunar surface to determine major elements, and minor elements during solar flares [4].

specifications.Detectors: Swept charge device X-ray sensors behind low-profile gold/copper collimators and aluminium/polycarbonate thin-film filters, operated near room temperature (no numeric value given) [4]
specifications.Protection: Deployable proton shield for passage through the radiation belts and major lunar-orbit particle events [4]
specifications.Target elements: Mg, Al and Si as primary elements; Ca, Ti and Fe as minor elements measured during solar flares [4]
specifications.XSM: Energy range 1 to 20 keV; field of view plus or minus 52 degrees; spectral sampling interval 16 s [4]
specifications.Mass: C1XS and XSM together 5.2 kg; not separated [4]
specifications.Power, dimensions, field of view (C1XS): Not given in the source reviewed [4]

examples.name: Chandrayaan-2 Large Area Soft X-ray Spectrometer (CLASS)
examples.type: Flown lunar orbital instrument on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter
examples.summary: CLASS is an X-ray fluorescence instrument for mapping lunar surface chemistry from the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter [5]. Its calibration, in-flight performance and first results were published in 2021 [6]. Its numerical design and flight parameters could not be verified from primary text in this run, so none are stated here.

specifications.Flight status: Flown; in-flight performance and first results reported in 2021 [6]
specifications.Mass, power, detectors, field of view: Not verified in this run; not publicly specified in the sources reviewed [5][6]

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions were not verified for any of the four examples. The Apollo instrument carried three proportional counters with beryllium windows and a separate solar monitor [2]. The SMART-1 and Chandrayaan-1 units use swept charge device sensors behind collimators and filters [3][4]. Overall enclosure dimensions for these units are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The collimator and field of view set the footprint that the instrument sees on the surface [2][3].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only verified mass figures are combined values: 5.2 kg for the SMART-1 D-CIXS together with its solar monitor [3], and 5.2 kg for the Chandrayaan-1 C1XS together with its solar monitor [4]. The mass of the Apollo XRFS and of CLASS was not verified in this run. Combined masses should not be read as the mass of the spectrometer alone.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: A power figure of 18 W is given in the SMART-1 mission table for D-CIXS together with its solar monitor [3]. No verified power figure was found for the Apollo XRFS, C1XS or CLASS in the sources reviewed [1][2][4].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: An orbital X-ray detector operates in vacuum, through large temperature swings between sunlight and eclipse, and in an environment with energetic particles. C1XS detectors operate near room temperature and use a deployable proton shield for radiation-belt passage and particle events [4]. Fluorescence measurements need a sunlit surface and sufficient solar X-ray input, so observation planning depends on solar activity [2][4]. Proportional counters depend on a stable gas fill and window; the Apollo 15 instrument showed gain shifts that led to a second window in the Apollo 16 solar monitor [2].
article.limitations: Fluorescence lines are detectable only within the detector energy range, so lighter elements and elements with weak lines are harder to measure. Measurements depend on solar X-ray input, which varies with solar activity. The Apollo 15 and 16 maps covered limited ground tracks at altitudes from tens to over a hundred kilometres [2]. Spatial resolution depends on altitude and collimator geometry; the Apollo low-altitude maps covered about 60 by 75 km [2]. Detector gain can drift, as observed on Apollo 15 [2]. Published mass and power figures are often for an instrument combined with its solar monitor [3][4].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The X-ray detectors described in this article are orbital instruments, so the relevant transport chain is spacecraft integration, launch, lunar transfer, lunar orbit insertion, commissioning and operation. Surface delivery and deployment do not apply to the examples reviewed.
transportation_process: Integrate the detector housing, collimators, filters and solar monitor on the spacecraft, with the viewing direction and the solar monitor's Sun view specified in advance.
Launch the spacecraft and transfer it to the Moon.
Insert the spacecraft into lunar orbit and commission the instrument, including checks of detector settings and calibration sources.
Operate in orbit with a fixed or nadir-pointed view so that the detector footprint covers the intended surface, using sunlit conditions for fluorescence measurements.
Manage radiation and thermal interfaces, for example the deployable proton shield on C1XS [4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The examples reviewed were not deployed on the surface. The Apollo 15 and 16 XRFS was mounted on the Command Service Module, and its solar monitor was placed on the opposite side of the module [1][2].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 15 and 16 XRFS on the Command Service Module [1][2]; SMART-1 D-CIXS with XSM [3]; Chandrayaan-1 C1XS with XSM [4]; Chandrayaan-2 CLASS [5][6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility of a new X-ray detector with any specific spacecraft or lander has not been assessed. It would depend on mass, dimensions, field-of-view and Sun-view requirements, thermal and radiation environment, and data interfaces, none of which has been matched here to a verified spacecraft specification.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 15 and 16 instruments mapped magnesium, aluminium and silicon from lunar orbit along their ground tracks [1][2]. A 2021 re-evaluation of their data updated the magnesium and aluminium values relative to silicon using improved instrument response and trajectory information [2]. SMART-1 D-CIXS and Chandrayaan-1 C1XS extended the approach with swept charge device detectors, with C1XS based primarily on D-CIXS [3][4]. Chandrayaan-2 CLASS follows on from C1XS [5][6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name 'X-ray detector' describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design, so the examples cannot be treated as interchangeable. Numerical values are tied to named instruments and sources. Several values could not be verified in this run: mass, power and dimensions for the Apollo XRFS; D-CIXS and XSM individually; C1XS power and dimensions; and all numerical design and flight parameters of CLASS. Design-stage values for D-CIXS may not match the flight unit. The journal of the 2021 Apollo re-evaluation is not verified here. The generic description of operating principles is engineering background, not a certified design specification for a new payload.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL query strings and fragments removed. No image objects are included in this run.
image_handling.note: No direct image asset URL was verified from an official page, so none is listed. See data_quality_notes.

data_quality_notes: Name is generic (a payload class). The four examples are specific instruments or designs and are not interchangeable.
No images were verified in this run. The image arrays are empty and no image URL is listed. Image research was not completed within the search budget.
Mass, power and dimension values are unverified for the Apollo XRFS, D-CIXS and XSM individually, C1XS power and dimensions, and CLASS. These are null or marked not publicly specified.
Conflicting D-CIXS mass: the ESA table gives 5.2 kg for D-CIXS with XSM. A secondary search summary cited 4.6 kg including the solar monitor from a 2003 paper. This was not verified and is not used.

D-CIXS resolution: the ESA table gives 50 km for the planned map product. A secondary search summary cited 42 km at 300 km altitude and 200 eV spectral resolution. This was not verified and is not used.

CLASS numerical parameters (detector count and area, energy range, footprint) came only from a secondary AI-generated digest. They are not used. The arXiv 1305.6218 PDF text and the Icarus 2021 abstract could not be read in this run.
C1XS detector count (24 SCD) came from a search summary of ESA archive material, not from a fetched page. It is not used.
The 2021 Apollo re-evaluation journal name was not verified; its received and accepted dates are taken from the paper itself.
Several sources could not be parsed or were blocked: the NTRS 1972 Apollo report, the ISSDC Chandrayaan-1 payload PDF (binary), the ADS abstract page (HTTP 405) and the Icarus page (HTTP 403).
